findings.label: Six timing cases are host-bound: the 1024-element call costs 10.77 us of device time inside a 70.02 us eval call, and the device stream idles ~70 us between consecutive kernels
findings.backend_detail: Ascend msprof op_summary + execution_trace for uniform-timing-0; Block Num = 4 for all 110 invocations.

findings.inference: Only about 15% of the complete 1024-element call is device execution. Because the 65536-element cases in the same round show the same ~0.070 ms eval latency (get_profile_context) while this 1024 case already costs 10.77 us on device, the residual ~59 us is per-call host work that does not scale with element count: output allocation (main.py:258), generator state read/advance (main.py:275-277) and the launch submission of the direct-entry closure (main.py:239-241). The direct-entry path demonstrably took effect (eval latency fell 0.1113 -> 0.0700 ms versus round 2 on this case), so the Triton metacall is no longer the dominant host term. The split inside the remaining ~59 us cannot be attributed with these artifacts: the timeline carries no host API durations and the msprof log reports no host summary, so naming allocation, generator state or launch submission as the single cause would be unsupported.

findings.label: Three 1M-element cases are device-bound and vector-pipe bound: eval latency equals kernel duration, vector ratio 0.88-0.90 with MTE2 ~0 and MTE3 <=2.5%
findings.backend_detail: Grid = cdiv(n, BLOCK*4) with BLOCK=4096 at 1M elements -> 64 programs; vector ratio is a marginal pipe-activity ratio, not peak utilization and not a time decomposition.

evidence.value: 64 in 110/110 invocations for each of timing-2 and timing-5 and timing-8

findings.inference: For these three cases eval latency and device duration coincide (85.25 vs 84.28; 87.99 vs 86.41; 86.91 vs 86.45 us), so host submission is fully overlapped and only device time matters. The kernel is arithmetic-bound in the vector pipe rather than bandwidth-bound: there are no input reads (MTE2 = 0.012 us) and MTE3 traffic of 1.3-2.1 us covers a 2 MiB output, which is far below this device's achievable bandwidth for an 84 us window. The work is the fully unrolled Philox4x32-10 (main.py:64-89, 10 static rounds with two mul_hi_lo splits each) plus uint_to_uniform_float scaling and a two-sided clamp (main.py:116-119). With vector busy 0.88-0.90 and scalar 7.4%, at most roughly 10% of the kernel window is not attributed to a busy pipe, so any device-side gain on these three cases must come from reducing arithmetic per element, not from more parallel programs or better DMA.

findings.label: The 1024-element case runs only 4 programs on a 20-core device, so per-program fixed cost dominates its 10.77 us device time
findings.backend_detail: num_sm reported by the service is 20 for Ascend910B4-1; 4 programs therefore use 4 of 20 vector cores.
findings.inference: _plan picks BLOCK = clamp(next_pow2(n/160), 64, 4096) = 64 and grid = cdiv(1024, 256) = 4, i.e. 256 elements per program on a 20-core device. Per-program vector plus scalar time is ~7.9 us for only 256 outputs, versus ~1.5 ns per output in the 1M regime, which indicates a large fixed per-program cost (unrolled Philox prologue and index setup) rather than element-proportional work. This makes finer program granularity tempting, but it cannot improve these cases in this round: the complete call is host-bound at 70 us, so reducing 10.77 us of device time changes nothing measurable.

findings.label: Large icache miss rate (13-18%) and intermittent +~6 us scalar spikes suggest instruction footprint is a secondary cost, but this is not yet localized
findings.backend_detail: No instruction/simulator artifact was collected; confidence is deliberately low.

evidence.metric: outlier invocations: task duration ~90.4-91.1 us with aiv_scalar_time 12.0-12.3 us vs steady-state 83.7-84.4 us / 6.15-6.20 us

findings.inference: The 10-round unrolled Philox plus four store paths is a large straight-line body, and the small case shows the higher instruction-cache miss rate. The occasional +6 us iterations where only scalar time grows could be instruction refetch or profiler/host interference. Both readings are consistent with an instruction-footprint effect, but no instruction-level artifact was collected in this round, so I do not treat this as a cause and would not act on it before the host question is resolved.

performance_interpretation: Round 3 splits the nine timing workloads into two regimes, so the frozen hypothesis is only half supported. Supported: for the six 1024/65536 cases the device work is small and the call is host-bound. timing-0 confirms it directly (10.77 us device inside a 70.02 us eval call, ~70 us of stream idle per invocation). Contradicted: for the three 1M-element cases the device kernel is 84.3-86.5 us and eval latency is 85.3/88.0/86.9 us, i.e. the call is device-bound; the hypothesis that all nine are launch-bound does not hold there. The eval-side numbers are also flat across dtype and size in the first two size classes (0.0693-0.0705 ms for 1024 and 65536 elements), which is itself evidence that a per-call host floor, not element count, sets those six latencies. Relative positioning versus the reference is therefore inverse to device work: the six host-bound cases are the round's wins (1.59-1.81x) and the three device-bound cases are the drag (1.13-1.28x), and the reference itself shows a flat ~0.096-0.127 ms floor. The largest remaining lever is the ~59 us unattributed host term (worth roughly +20-25% geo_mean if even 20 us of it is removable), because the device-bound cases expose at most ~10% unaccounted vector/scalar slack and reducing Philox arithmetic would require changing generator semantics, which the campaign forbids. All timings above are diagnostic; authoritative latency remains the get_profile_context walltime (geo_mean 1.4926, before 0.8924).

next_experiment.action_description: Attribute and then remove the per-call host cost of the six launch-bound cases. First run one bounded ablation probe under the same KGS complete-call timer on the frozen timing inputs (FP16 1024 and 65536, plus one dtype variant), measuring the current path against three mutually exclusive ablations of the host prologue in main.py: (a) output allocation at line 258 replaced by a preallocated scratch buffer, (b) the three generator-state calls at lines 275-277 replaced by constants, (c) the direct launch submission at lines 239-241 replaced by the ordinary metacall as control. These ablations are diagnostic only and must never be delivered: no cached output buffers, no fixed seed or offset, no input mutation. Then deliver exactly one change to the component whose ablation shows the largest reduction, keeping the per-call current-stream read, the real per-call offset advance of grid*block, and a genuinely new returned tensor. If no ablation exceeds a few microseconds, stop host work and record the launch floor as measured rather than guessed.
next_experiment.expected_impact: If allocation plus generator state account for ~20 us of the ~59 us host term, the six host-bound cases move from 0.0693-0.0705 ms to roughly 0.048-0.050 ms, taking each from 1.59-1.81x to about 2.2-2.4x and lifting geo_mean from 1.4926 to about 1.8 (+20-25%). The three device-bound cases (85.3-88.0 us, driven by 84.3-86.5 us of kernel time) should be unchanged, since host time is already fully overlapped there. If the launch submission dominates the host term, expected gain is near zero and the probe result itself becomes the deliverable evidence.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Risk: an ablation reading leaks into the delivered source and breaks the generator contract (fixed seed/offset, no state advance, cached output tensor) or aliases the caller's buffer; the 18 interval/statistics checks and the 3 seed/offset high-bit plus replay checks would catch this, and they must pass before any formal eval. Risk: probe timing is measured under different conditions than the eval and is over-read; keep all ablations inside one process with the same inputs and report the control alongside. Risk: removing allocation via an allocator fast path could change the returned tensor's identity or strides. Rollback is a byte-level restore of round-3 source (sha256 cd711114eb3fc94b2b791c92371569e77fca0850d33428421822cb557978e1a9); if the delivered change does not beat 1.4926 geo_mean with no per-case latency regression, restore it.
success_criteria: All 9 correctness and 9 timing workloads report PASSED in a full KGS eval of the new executed bytes.
Headline geo_mean strictly exceeds the round-3 value 1.4926084127327262, with the six 1024/65536 cases individually faster than 0.0693-0.0705 ms and no regression on timing-2/5/8.

The 18 interval/statistics semantics checks plus the 3 generator checks (seed bits 31/32/40, offset bits 31/32/40, state advance and restore-replay) pass, proving the per-call offset still advances by grid*block and is not cached or fixed.

The probe table shows for each of allocation, generator state and launch submission a measured delta; the delivered change is the one whose ablation moved the complete call, and that same ablation delta is re-observed after the change.

warnings: Profiler timings (msprof op_summary, execution timeline) are diagnostic and are not eval latency; all speedup and latency numbers above come from get_profile_context.

op_summary aggregates 10 warmup invocations plus 100 measured ones for this campaign; the first rows in the CSV are larger (e.g. 25.6 and 171.6 us) and are excluded from the reported averages, so CSV row count must not be read as the measured sample.

No host-side API tracing is available: the msprof log reports that the host directory was analyzed but has no summary data to export, so the split of the ~59 us host term is not attributable from these artifacts.
Vector/scalar/MTE ratios are marginal pipe-activity fractions and overlap in time; they are not a time decomposition and not a peak-utilization figure, so no Roofline number is claimed.
The 1M-element CSVs contain a few invocations (~4 of 110) with ~+6 us scalar time and ~+6 us duration; I did not treat these as a stable effect.
open_questions: How much of the ~59 us per-call host cost at 1024/65536 elements is output allocation, generator state read/advance, and backend launch submission respectively?
Would more than 64 programs reduce the 84-86 us device time at 1M elements, given that vector is already 0.88-0.90 busy and scalar only 7.4%?

Is the 13-18% icache miss rate plus the intermittent scalar spikes an instruction-footprint effect of the unrolled 10-round Philox, or profiler/host interference? Resolving it needs an instruction-level artifact, which this round did not collect.

Are the six host-bound latencies already at the minimum achievable per-call submission cost of this backend, i.e. is the reference's ~0.096-0.127 ms floor also dominated by three host submissions (two memcpys plus one aclnn call) rather than by its device work?
